newsitem.title: UK: Esso says Pricewatch cut '96 retail earnings.
newsitem.headline: Esso says Pricewatch cut '96 retail earnings.

text.p: Esso Petroleum's Pricewatch campaign cut into its 1996 retail earnings but the giant oil company remains committed to its year-old programme that rattled the domestic gasoline market and squeezed margins, an Esso retailing official said.

Esso's market share returned toward its historical levels after matching -- but not undercutting -- its lowest priced competitors last year, keeping U.K. pump prices amongst the lowest in Europe, Mark Cash, retail planning and economics manager, told Reuters in an interview.

"Our 1996 retail earnings will be down versus 1995 because I think everyone recognises that margins were tighter," Cash said, without giving 1995 figures nor commenting on expectations for this year's earnings.
Wood Mackenzie consultants estimated in 1996 it cost Esso 200 million sterling ($334.4 million), or about one-third of Esso U.K.'s pre-tax profits in 1995.
That takes into account the drop in gross margins and a boost in Esso's market share to 20 percent from 17 percent.

"We never instigated undercutting of prices. We've only matched prices in the market, and, yes, we will continue to do that," he said. "We have no plans to change Pricewatch. It's a long-term strategic marketing change we made in 1996 and we plan to stay with it."

Esso, a subsidiary of U.S. oil major Exxon Corp, pledged to monitor supermarket prices within three miles and other stations within one mile of its sites nationwide, and normally match the lowest price.
Cash said 75 percent of the U.K. population lives within two miles of one of its more than 2,000 service stations, making it the retail market leader.
An estimated one million more motorists a week, based on figures in July, were filling up at Esso stations in 1996 than in 1995, Cash said, describing Pricewatch as "very successful" last year.

That confirmed its research that most consumers were primarily interested low prices and not necessarily promotions. He said that "...unless we respond to what the consumers want, we cannot survive long term and neither can our competitors survive long term."
"Yes, we have gained market share," he added, without elaborating.

But Esso, in a press release at the launch of Pricewatch, said it served 34,000 customers per hour, 365 days a year, and then later in 1996 said that 40,000 customers stopped at its filling stations every hour.

The ensuing price war shaved gross fuel margins for the industry to as low as two pence per litre last summer by some accounts, sparking industry estimates that up to 2,000 filling stations could close in 1996.

It also prompted a Parliamentary inquiry into whether consumers were enjoying "unrealistically low prices" that would quicken site closures, reduce competition and eventually lead to higher pump prices.

The Trade and Industry Committee is expected to comment this month on a hearing in December where the government and the Office of Fair Trading were criticised for ignoring its recommendations issued last summer.
Many industry analysts, however, have argued the domestic market is rife with overcapacity -- the U.K. is a traditional exporter of gasoline -- that meant a war of attrition was inevitable.
Cash said Esso agreed with two of the committee's conclusions, that the retail market remains highly competitive and that government intervention was not necessary.
"There are very low barriers to entry and therefore it remains a highly competitive market," he said.
"There have always been site closings and it has been an unfortunate fact of life," he said.
($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
